text:
Scrap the Parking Mandates

Every city has a building that could not be built today. It might be the corner bakery with apartments above it, the narrow rowhouse on a small lot, or the old main street that tourists photograph. These places are often the best-loved parts of town, and in most cities they are illegal to replicate, because none of them provide the number of parking spaces the zoning code demands. That alone should make us suspicious of the rule. Cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning codes entirely.

Start with where the numbers come from. Parking minimums prescribe a fixed quantity of off-street spaces per unit of something: two per dwelling, one per 200 square feet of restaurant, one per three seats in a funeral parlour. These ratios carry an air of engineering precision, but they are mostly borrowed from neighbouring towns or drawn from surveys of peak demand at isolated suburban sites where parking was free and nobody could arrive any other way. The planner Donald Shoup, who spent decades studying the subject, called the practice pseudoscience. A rule built to accommodate the busiest hour of the busiest day, at a site with no alternative to driving, will produce a surplus everywhere else. Anyone who has walked across a half-empty retail car park on an ordinary Tuesday has seen the result.

That surplus is expensive. A surface space costs thousands of dollars to build once land is counted, and a space in a structured or underground garage commonly runs into the tens of thousands. The cost does not disappear because drivers pay nothing at the kerb. It is folded into rents, restaurant bills and shop prices, where it is paid by everyone, including people who do not own a car. Those people are disproportionately poor, young, old or disabled. A tenant without a car who rents a flat with a mandated space is subsidising a neighbour's second vehicle. It is hard to design a more regressive transfer on purpose.

The mandates also suppress housing. On a small urban lot, the parking requirement often determines how many homes fit, not the height limit or the setbacks. A developer who could build twelve flats builds eight because the site cannot hold twelve spaces, or builds nothing because the garage makes the numbers fail. Small infill projects, the kind that add homes without changing a street's character, are hit hardest. Converting an empty office or an old warehouse to housing can be blocked for the same reason: the building exists, the demand exists, and the parking cannot be conjured. In cities struggling with housing costs, a rule that swaps homes for car storage is a strange thing to keep.

Then there is what the mandates do to the shape of a city. Requiring every building to sit in its own pool of asphalt spreads destinations apart, and distance makes walking impractical, buses inefficient and cycling unpleasant. People then drive because they have to, which appears to confirm that all the parking was needed. The requirement manufactures the demand it claims to measure. The asphalt itself adds stormwater runoff and summer heat, and the extra driving adds emissions and congestion.

The strongest objection is spillover. If new buildings supply less parking, residents fear that cars will flood nearby streets. The concern is reasonable, but it is an argument about managing kerb space, and cities have tools for that: permit zones, time limits, and meters priced so that a space or two is usually free on each block. Shoup's suggestion of returning meter revenue to the street that generates it, for pavements, trees and cleaning, gives residents a reason to welcome that pricing. Forcing every builder in the city to over-supply parking in order to protect free kerb space is the costliest possible solution to a problem that can be solved with signs and a price.

It also matters what abolition does not do. Removing a minimum is not imposing a maximum. Developers will still build parking where customers and tenants want it, because unlettable flats and empty shops are bad business. Lenders will still insist on it where the market expects it. What changes is who decides: the people with money at stake and knowledge of the site, in place of a table copied from a code written decades ago. Accessible spaces for disabled people can and should remain mandated separately.

Nor is this an untested idea. Buffalo dropped its minimums citywide in 2017, and Minneapolis, San Francisco, Austin and others have followed, along with a growing list of small towns. The reported results are undramatic: new projects generally still include parking, often less than the old rules required, and housing gets built on sites that had sat idle. The predicted chaos has not arrived.

A good planning rule prevents a harm that markets and neighbours cannot sort out themselves. Parking minimums do the reverse. They compel an expense, hide its cost, and hand the bill to those least able to pay. Cities should delete them and manage their streets directly.
